answer:
1. The animation compares buying and renting using US history from January 1991 on. It uses a grid of tiles, one for each possible starting month, 247 in all. A lit tile means the buyer was ahead after the holding period. A dark tile means the renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. A small figure named Nina, labeled illustrative, stands between an apartment and a house.

2. The holding period changes. At 15 years, every one of the 247 start months is lit, so the buyer was ahead every time, and the weakest case still left the buyer $79,829 ahead. At ten years, a dark band of renter-ahead months appears in the middle of the grid. At fifteen years, the grid is fully lit again. In the last two frames the scene moves to Nina. Her stay is labeled "unknown", and the rent tag on the apartment is labeled "unchanged".

3. The result depends on how long you stay. Over 15-year holds in this history, buying beat renting in every starting month. Over ten-year holds, some start months favored renting. Nina's uncertain stay shows that the outcome depends on a fact the buyer doesn't know in advance. The footers "US only · history, not a forecast" and "ILLUSTRATIVE" say this is past data and not a prediction.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer would probably take away that buying has historically paid off over long holds, and that a short or uncertain stay carries more risk. The animation doesn't say that in words, and it doesn't tell anyone to buy or rent.

5. The picture and on-screen text show the historical pattern (all lit at 15 years, a dark band at ten) and the "unknown" stay length. The takeaway about long holds and uncertain stays is my own reading. The animation never states any advice, and its "not a forecast" label cuts against treating it as a recommendation.
